claims.text: The baseline material is a nanocrystalline WTaCrVHf refractory high-entropy alloy produced by powder metallurgy.
Increasing the Hf content by 2–5 at.% will enhance local lattice strain and lattice distortion in WTaCrVHf.
Augmented lattice distortion disrupts one-dimensional defect-migration pathways.
Disruption of one-dimensional migration shifts radiation-induced defect motion toward isotropic three-dimensional diffusion.
Short-range three-dimensional defect motion increases vacancy–interstitial recombination.
Greater vacancy–interstitial recombination reduces the concentration of surviving radiation-induced defects.
Altered defect migration and enhanced recombination reduce defect clustering and suppress void swelling.
The Hf-modified WTaCrVHf alloy will have 30–50% lower defect density than the baseline after irradiation.
The Hf-modified WTaCrVHf alloy will have 30–50% less void swelling than the baseline after irradiation.
Increasing Hf by 2–5 at.% will preserve strength at a level comparable to or better than the unmodified alloy.
Increasing Hf by 2–5 at.% will preserve ductility at a level comparable to or better than the unmodified alloy.
The proposed beneficial effect will hold under plasma-facing irradiation at approximately 500–800 °C.
Combined Ar+, He+, and D+ implantation is relevant to testing materials for fusion applications.
At higher added-Hf concentrations, phase changes or Hf segregation may limit the beneficial effect.

Prior experimental and simulation work supports the general proposition that alloy complexity and lattice distortion can alter defect migration, enhance recombination, and improve radiation tolerance.
